I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01031

“And here is the least that can be said of it all. Having perceived spiritual truth within both groups in question—the Shiites and the Sufis—I came to see what was true and what was negative in each; in what way and in what sense each group was right and had something positive to offer; and in what way and in what sense each was wrong and had something negative to answer for.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01032

“I understood how both are directed toward the central point, the gnostic truth of Tawhîd, just as rays converge from the circumference upon the center. Then I understood the hidden meaning of His words: ‘There is not a single creature whom He does not hold by the forelock; my Lord stands upon a straight path’ (21:59); and of these: ‘Each has a region of Heaven toward which he turns in prayer’ (2:143); and again: ‘To God belong East and West. Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God’ (2:109).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01033

“Then too I understood the secret of this saying of our Prophet: ‘The paths toward God are as numerous as the breaths of creatures’; and of this other saying of our First Imam: ‘Knowledge is a single point; it is the ignorance of the ignorant that multiplies it.’
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01034

“And so I became like a substance ready to receive the forms of every belief (...) Verse [by Ibn ’Arabî]: ‘My heart has become capable of every form— / A meadow for gazelles and a monastery for Christian monks, / A temple for idols and the pilgrim’s Kaaba, / The tablets of the Torah and the book of the Quran. / I follow the religion of Love, and wherever its mount may turn, / Love is my religion and my faith.’
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01035

“Certainly there can be no doubt that this—by which I mean the affirmation of the truth of Sufism—will be a hard blow (ya’sob) to the minds of certain Shiites from whom the truth remains veiled. They will imagine that I am lending the support of error to the school of those who trade in error (ahl al-bâtil), and that I am trying, without right or reason, to prove that such people possess the truth.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01036

“But that is not at all what I am doing. In truth, I am supporting only the school of my fathers and forefathers, the immaculate Imams, and I do so from both the outward and the inward points of view, as I said earlier.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01037

“For most Sufis themselves, out of ignorance, imagine that the immaculate Imams lacked this supreme distinction—by which I mean their privileged knowledge of the Higher Sciences. And there are Shiites who make the same mistake when they imagine that the excellence of their Imams was confined to the ordinary knowledge current among the Shiites themselves. Nothing could be further from the truth. Each of the two groups (Shiites who are not Sufis and Sufis who are not Shiites) is mistaken in its understanding of things. Both miss the mark through the ideas they entertain. May God preserve us from falling into the error they share!
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01038

“There is no knowledge of which the holy Imams are not the source, no secret of spiritual knowledge of which they are not the treasury. They stand at the head of the scholars of the religious Law (sharî’at); they guide those who follow the mystical Path (tarîqat); they are the spiritual poles (aqtâb) of those who uphold the knowledge of ultimate truth (haqîqat). They are God's representatives in His earth and His heaven, the forms in which His sublimity and majesty appear (mazâhir), both in the world visible to the senses (molk) and in the world beyond the senses (Malakût). I call God to witness!
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01039

“Had it not been for them, the vault of the heavens would never have been raised, the earth would never have been made firm, and no creatures would exist in heaven or on earth. This is confirmed by the inspired tradition in which God says to His Prophet: ‘Had it not been for you, I would not have created the heavenly spheres […]’” Moreover, the fact that Mohammad and his descendants, the twelve Imams, are one Soul and one Essence, and therefore deserve the same faith as Mohammad himself, is a manifest truth that no one can fail to see. It rests on three foundations—philosophical, theological, and theosophical—as you will learn in the course of this book.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01040

“It is likewise well known that, according to the mystical theosophers, the entire universe is sustained by the primordial reality of the Perfect Human Being (al-Insân al-Kâmil, Anthropos teleios), and that the heavenly spheres revolve through the breaths of his breathing. This is what the shaykh (Ibn ’Arabî) shows in his treatise Noskhat al-Haqq. At the beginning of his introductory address (khotbat) he writes: ‘Glory to God, who established the Perfect Human Being as the teacher of the visible world (mo’allim al-molk), and who makes heaven revolve through the breaths of his breathing,’ and so on. Now, by common agreement, and from the philosophical, theological, and theosophical points of view alike, nothing in the human world is more perfect than those we have just named.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01041

“The proof is this: the human being is the noblest and most perfect of existing beings; among human beings, the prophets are the noblest, followed by the Awliyâ, the Friends of God. And, again by common agreement, our Prophet and his descendants are the noblest among the prophets and the Friends of God.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01042

“Thus he and the twelve Imams are the noblest and most exalted of all beings, the very quintessence and perfection of everything in the universe. Above all, this is true of the one who was the soul of our Prophet (nafsot, his very ‘self’) and his successor: our first Imam. In his Khotbat al-Iftikhâr he declared plainly: ‘I am the Sign of the All-Powerful. I am the essence of the Mysteries. I am the Guide of the Heavens. I am familiar with the radiance of divine Majesty.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01043

“I am the intimate of Gabriel. I am the chosen one of Michael. I am the prince of the Angels. I am the support of the Spheres. I am true to my promises. I am the guardian of the thunderbolt. I am the lightning that flashes. I am the lofty vault ...’ and, later: ‘I am the Face of God. I am the side of God. I am the hand of God. I am the First. I am the Last. I am the Manifest. I am the Hidden.’”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01044

Haydar Âmolî then quotes the long hadîth reported by Akhtab Khwârezmî, particularly revealing in its implications for the doctrines of the Imam and of Christ. Addressing the Imam, the Prophet explains that he refrains from saying certain things for fear that people will make the same mistake about the Imam that Christians made about Jesus: “It is enough for you to know that you are part of me just as I am part of you, and that you stand in relation to me as Aaron stood in relation to Moses, with this difference: after me there will be no prophet.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01045

The author then explains why, in good conscience, he could not refuse the urgent request made by his friends, and how he came to write this book. He sketches its program in a dozen points and then presents a clearer outline in a comprehensive table. We have summarized that plan above. The prologue (fâtihat) is followed by a long introduction (moqaddama), explaining why the secrets entrusted to this book must be guarded against the curiosity of the uninitiated.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01046
Let us translate one more passage, the closing paragraph of the prologue, whose tone is in harmony with the whole work.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01047

“What is asked here of the Masters, of those who are the pillars among people of genuine mystical experience—indeed, what is demanded of those who are the kings and princes among the masters of inward contemplation—is that they look upon this book with a view to improving and correcting it, not with an indulgence that deliberately turns a blind eye. Let them treat this book as a shaykh treats his pupil, not as a lover treats his beloved, seeing nothing but her virtues. For in truth the fruits of this book will belong to no one but themselves.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01048

“As God says: ‘The effort of anyone who does good works while remaining a faithful believer will not be met with ingratitude. Truly, We shall write it down’ (21:94). In the end it is they themselves who will benefit from this book, through the depth of their own understanding. As God also says: ‘I shall not allow the work of any one of you, man or woman, to be lost in vain’ (3:193).”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01049

We shall now translate a few passages from the book's conclusion. The author explains why he sometimes wrote in Arabic and sometimes in Persian. He then addresses the Sufis and the Shiites once more, clarifying whom he means by these names and reminding both groups of the conclusion already placed before them at the beginning of the book.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01050
Finally comes the very last page. Here a motif from one of Ibn ’Arabî's best-known poems returns, resolving every discord like the closing phrase of a great orchestral composition.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01051

“Just as the word of God is not truly divided by the difference between languages, although it appears to be divided when expressed in Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, and so on, the words of the theosophers are not truly divided by their different ways of speaking or by the variety of languages they use, whether Arabic, Persian, Indian, or Greek. So the author should not be reproached here for shortcomings of language or weaknesses of composition. He himself acknowledges them and asks pardon for them ...
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01052

“Moreover, if those who requested this book had not been familiar with Arabic, the author would not have treated his subject in Arabic. He has simply expressed his thoughts in the language required by those who asked him to write, because they were familiar with it and could understand it readily […]. That is why I have written a number of books and treatises in Persian when those requesting them were Persians and asked me to write in Persian […].
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01053

“One more thing. When you hear me speak of Sufis, do not assume, before learning their principles and fundamental doctrines, that I mean the Sufis of the present day. They are no more Sufis in the true sense than the scholars of our time are scholars in the true sense. No: whenever the subject of the Sufis comes to a reader's mind, or the reader hears someone speak of them, or learns about them from books, let the names that come to mind be those of the earliest, most learned, and most eminent Sufis: Salmân Fârsî, Oways al-Qaranî, the Ahl al-Soffa, and others; Miqdâd, Abû Dharr, ’Ammâr; and, after them, Komayl ibn Ziyâd, Abû Yazîd Bastâmî, and Jonayd Baghdâdî. These were disciples and pupils of the immaculate Imams, entrusted with their secrets, as I explained to you in the first chapter.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01054

In the same way, addressing the Shiites, our Sayyed specifies whom he has in mind: the Twelver Imami Shiites, to the exclusion of the other branches of Shiism. For in matters of fundamental doctrine (osûl), the Imamis base their teaching on the divinely authorized designation (nass) and impeccability (’ismat) of the Imams; in matters of practical application (forû’), their traditions rest on authentic transmission from the Prophet and the Imams. They are the people of whom it is said: “God will raise up people whom He will love and who will love Him” (5:69, §1292). The final pages then recapitulate the arguments sustained throughout the Jâmi’ al-asrâr. There are those we might call Shiites and Sufis in the ordinary, limited sense. At the very least, they ought to respect one another and recognize how they complement each other.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01055

But this peaceful reconciliation is only a first step. From there the final conclusion gathers together the teaching of the entire book, defining once again what it means to be a Shiite in the fullest and truest sense.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01056

“What gives the two groups (Imami Shiites and Sufis) their dignity, determines their rank, or, more precisely, constitutes their spiritual truth, is that both bear the secrets of the prophets and the Awliyâ, in their outward and inward dimensions alike. For the prophets and the Awliyâ possessed all the divine secrets, outwardly and inwardly. The Shiites safeguard their teachings and secrets in their outward aspect, according to the religious Law (sharî’at), while the Sufis safeguard their teachings and secrets in their inward aspect, according to spiritual truth (haqîqat).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01057
“Yet in reality the Sufis are themselves also the Shiites, as I made clear when explaining the difference between the believer who has been put to the test and the believer who has not.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01058

This is indeed the decisive question that Haydar Âmolî has explored at length in his book, relying above all on the traditions of the holy Imams. The believer who has been put to the test is the Shiite in the fullest sense—not the merely outward Shiite mentioned above, content with the external forms of religion. Nor is this believer the merely nominal Sufi who rails against the Shiites because he has forgotten the origins of his khirqa, the Sufi cloak of initiation, and forgotten that the first Sufis were disciples of the Imams.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01059

A few lines earlier, Haydar Âmolî again recalled who the true Sufis were. He might have added Sa’d Hamûyeh to their number, since he quotes him and must have known of his personal devotion to the Hidden Imam. The point remains that the notion of the “believer who has been put to the test” is what makes it possible to overcome the confrontation between Shiism and Sufism, by recalling their origins. The spiritual type that emerges—the Shiite in the fullest sense—is precisely the kind of person Haydar Âmolî, judging by the book's opening, believes himself to represent in this world. He knows that others around him aspire to the same ideal.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01060

Indeed, certain brothers asked him to compose the Jâmi’ al-asrâr precisely because they had recognized in him this spirituality of integral Shiism, uniting sharî’at and haqîqat, the outward and the inward, and doing nothing other than putting the complete teaching of the holy Imams into practice. What must be overcome is a prejudice shared by the ordinary Shiites and the Sunni Sufis (who are, in a sense, without knowing it, representatives of Shiism in partibus Sunnitarum—within Sunni territory): the belief that the holy Imams did not possess the knowledge of the higher sciences.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01061

Sayyed Haydar speaks for all the Shiite gnostics (’orafâ) when he declares that, in truth, “there is no knowledge of which the holy Imams are not the source, no secret of spiritual knowledge of which they are not the treasury. They stand at the head of the scholars of the religious Law (sharî’at); they guide those who follow the mystical Path (tarîqat); they are the poles of those who journey toward the knowledge of ultimate truth (haqîqat).”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01062

More than this: when a Shiite theosopher speaks in such terms, he is not thinking of the Imams merely as historical individuals, of their brief appearance in earthly history. He means their eternal, pre-cosmic reality, their place within the fullness of the eternal Muhammadan Reality (Haqîqat mohammadîya). “They are,” writes Haydar Âmolî, “God's representatives in His earth and His heaven; they are the forms in which His sublimity and majesty appear (mazâhir), in the world visible to the senses (Molk) and the world beyond the senses (Malakût).” This is why the Shiite condemns himself to fall short of his own spiritual calling as long as he fails to realize the complete ideal of spiritual life offered from the beginning by the holy Imams.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01063

Haydar Âmolî feels himself to be neither an innovator nor an isolated figure. The hadîths he draws upon throughout his books assure him that he is a faithful interpreter of the Imams' complete teaching. The spiritual ideal he sought to embody in his life and in his own person, even to the point of making the heart-rending decision demanded by his vocation, is the type of spirituality we find so richly represented, in all its variety, throughout Iranian Shiism, among figures such as Mîr Dâmâd, Sadrâ Shîrâzî, Mohsen Fayz, Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î, and many others.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01064

“One should judge the personal faith professed by the author of this book only in light of the standpoint he has maintained from beginning to end, and only after reflecting on it and studying it as carefully as it deserves. What I mean is that the author asks to be recognized solely as someone who gathers together the secrets of the prophets and the Awliyâ in both their outward and inward aspects—what are called, respectively, the sharî’at, the tarîqat, and the haqîqat—and thus as someone who has truly achieved the union of outward and inward. This is the most perfect position, the highest degree, referred to so often in these pages.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01065

“The author therefore counts himself neither among the Shiites in the ordinary sense nor among the Sufis in the ordinary sense, but as one who belongs to the Muhammadan station (maqâm mohammadî), the station that unites both the outward and the inward. The Prophet said: ‘My direction of prayer (qibla) lies between East and West.’ This is what the following verse calls the eternal religion (Dîn qayyim): ‘This is the eternal religion, but most people do not know it’ (12:40), for everything else is merely opinion concerning religion […]. That is why, speaking of this way, I repeat what the most profound and eminent of men has said, in these very words: ‘This is my way; it is straight; follow it’ (6:154) ...
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01066

“I shall say again at the end of this book what I said at the beginning, for the final things are a return to the origins. With these words I shall bring the book to a close—with this poem (by Ibn ’Arabî):
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01067

“Until this day I rejected my companion Whenever his faith was not the faith of my heart. Now my heart has become capable of every form: It is a meadow for gazelles, a monastery for Christian monks, A temple for idols, the pilgrim's Kaaba, The tablets of the Torah and the book of the Qur'an. I follow the religion of love; wherever its mount may turn, Love is my religion and my faith.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01068

It is as though this celebrated poem of Ibn ’Arabî were, for our Sayyed, the secret confession of faith of the “believer who has been put to the test,” of the “Shiite in the fullest sense,” and also the sign of Ibn ’Arabî's integration into Shiite spiritual knowledge. Its return at the end of a book filled with demanding philosophical and theosophical discussions is profoundly characteristic of Haydar Âmolî's manner—a manner that, as we have suggested, employs almost unknowingly a masterly form of orchestration. To anyone who presses these questions too bluntly, the returning poem offers the answer of a musical phrase. It says what it has to say without putting it into explanatory words, which in any case could never say it.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
en-book-4-ch-1-s4
4. Theological Tawhîd and Ontological Tawhîd
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01069
Our analysis of the Jâmi’ al-asrâr has shown that the first two of its three books are devoted to the theosophy of Tawhîd, the affirmation of divine oneness.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01070

Yet there is no imbalance here. For the author, every theme of theosophy—the questions of prophecy and the Imams, as well as the theory of knowledge and its stages corresponding to the levels of sharî’at, tarîqat, and haqîqat—is simply an implication or application of the doctrine of Tawhîd. That doctrine itself explains and justifies the distinction between theological or outward Tawhîd and ontological or inward Tawhîd. Haydar Âmolî is anxious to make his meaning clear:
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01071

“In the plan I have just set out,” he writes, “there is a hidden intention addressed to the spiritual elite. I mean a secret that will not escape anyone worthy of understanding it, for a hint is enough for a person of higher understanding. If I have added the subjects of sharî’at, tarîqat, and haqîqat, and the other subjects treated specifically in Book III, to the subject of Tawhîd and its different forms—even though this work is essentially devoted to Tawhîd—there is a reason.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01072

“First, there is no mystery deeper than the hidden mystery of Tawhîd, with all its consequences and implications. It is this mystery we must bring to light, and by it we must find our bearings. Indeed, those who asked me to write this book asked for nothing else.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01073

“But there was a second reason for discussing the theosophical secrets reserved for Book III. Tawhîd contains difficulties and subtleties that belong to different levels: some to the level of those who follow the outward religious Law (sharî’at), others to that of those who set out along the mystical Path (tarîqat), and still others to that of those who have attained spiritual truth (haqîqat). Only someone whose understanding has reached the appropriate level can grasp what these distinctions mean. I needed to explain the degrees and levels of Tawhîd, so that people might understand its true meaning and stop condemning one another.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01074

“If, then, we had to discuss nobowwat (the prophetic vocation), risâlat (the mission of the prophet who is sent as a messenger), and walâyat (the Imam's spiritual authority and gift), it was because these are the source from which everything springs and unfolds. Tawhîd proceeds from them alone, and it is made manifest only through those who bear them: the prophet, the messenger, and the Imam. It was therefore essential to acquire a spiritual understanding (ma’rifat) of these three things. The same applies to divine communication, inspiration, and inward revelation (the third qâ’ida of Book III), and to the concepts of Islâm, imân, and iqân (the fourth qâ’ida), because all of them follow from and are implied in the first three.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01075

“In truth, all these subjects make up a single subject. So closely are they bound together that, if even one question were neglected, the whole problem could not appear as it should; its solution would remain hidden from understanding, as anyone who grasps these matters will recognize. The strongest reason for the plan of this work, therefore, is that explaining Tawhîd requires us also to speak of those who profess it. The whole work consequently treats Tawhîd itself in Books I and II, and then those who profess it in Book III. There is, in truth, no other way of proceeding” (§§27–30 of our edition).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01076

With this framework established, Haydar Âmolî develops the theosophy of Tawhîd, the affirmation of the One, in complete fidelity to Ibn ’Arabî's teaching. But the argument inevitably leads to the doctrines of prophecy and the Imams, and to the idea of the cycle of walâyat: the period of spiritual initiation through the Friends of God, succeeding the period in which prophets brought religious laws.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01077

At this point, as we have already indicated, our Sayyed's loyalty to the Ibn ’Arabî he so admires must give way to a still more pressing obligation: fidelity to the teaching of the Imams of Twelver Shiism. Much to his regret, he will have to direct a fundamental criticism against Ibn ’Arabî. By giving Jesus, rather than the Imam, the title “Seal of walâyat,” Ibn ’Arabî shakes the entire structure of the doctrines of prophecy and the Imams.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01078

The questions raised by Tawhîd lead us back to the remarkable Qur'anic verse that Haydar Âmolî interprets in a passage discussed earlier (Book I, Chapter III, 2), as an example of what we called the “spiritual struggle of Shiism.” In that verse our Sayyed “read” the eternal calling of Shiism—that is, of inward or esoteric Islam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01079

Whenever this calling finds expression, we hear the same underlying note. It sounds in the interpretation of the verse concerning the Divine Trust (33:72); it sounds, as we have seen, in Adam's reply to the unknown questioner, “I knew nothing other than God”; and it sounds in the final words of the last visible representative of the Hidden Imam, ’Alî al-Samarî: “From now on, the matter belongs to God alone.” It is one and the same spirit, combining unshakable trust with radical pessimism. This same spirit vibrates throughout the pages in which Haydar Âmolî explains the Islamic profession of faith: Lâ ilâha illâ’Llâh—there is no god but God (Non deus nisi Deus).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01080

The essential point is this. By taking upon himself the trust of the divine secret, as we have been told, Adam did violence to himself, to his own “soul.” He erased his individual self within the divine Selfhood and henceforth knew nothing other than God.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01081

But did a human being have the power to assume this trust, which all other beings had refused? In fact, Adam anticipated and claimed for himself what could only be the privilege of the last Imam. The complete realization of Tawhîd, uniting its theological and ontological forms, can occur only together with the complete manifestation of walâyat. That manifestation cannot come about until the Twelfth Imam reappears from his concealment as the Imam of the Resurrection. Adam's sublime act of violence against himself and his sublime ignorance of everything but God turned against humanity. They degenerated into oppression and folly, because human beings would inevitably come to regard something other than God as real in its own right. This is precisely what is at stake in Tawhîd, in bearing witness to the One.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01082

On the face of it, nothing could be simpler than the Islamic profession of faith: Lâ ilâha illâ’Llâh. It seems to affirm that, on one side, there is one God, and, on the other, the multitude of beings He has created. In reality nothing is more difficult. Even this apparently straightforward explanation, meant for everyone, shows how a naïve understanding of Tawhîd already thinks in terms of something other than God. That is why Tawhîd has occupied the efforts of successive generations of thinkers in Islam, just as it has absorbed the meditations of the mystics.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01083

Ismaili theosophy, for example, found a way beyond the problem through a powerful dialectic, showing that outward monotheism, at the very moment when it believes itself to be exalting the One and setting Him apart, falls into the worst kind of metaphysical idolatry. This is exactly the danger and illusion Haydar Âmolî denounces. For the relationship between uncreated Being (Ens increatum) and created being (Ens creatum) can be approached as it ought to be only through an inward, esoteric teaching.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01084

How far the matter is from being simple—how the very secret of Tawhîd is the secret Adam took upon himself at such terrible risk—is suggested by an exclamation attributed to ’Abdollâh ibn ’Abbâs, one of the Prophet's most famous companions despite his youth. His importance lies in the statements reported from him, which make it possible to trace certain mystical interpretations of Qur'anic verses back to the Prophet's own circle.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01085

Concerning the verse “God is He who created the seven heavens and as many earths” (65:12), Haydar Âmolî recalls that ’Abdollâh ibn ’Abbâs was once standing on Mount ’Arafât, twelve miles from Mecca, on the ninth day of Dhû’l-Hijja, the day of ’arafa during the pilgrimage. Raising his staff, he cried aloud: “People! If I were to explain this verse to you as I heard the Prophet himself explain it, you would stone me.” (Here we should remember the poem in which the Fourth Imam declared that he, too, was unable to reveal the secret of spiritual knowledge.) When explaining the verse privately to his close companions, ’Abdollâh ibn ’Abbâs referred to another: “God is the One” (112:1).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01086

Through this divine aloneness, this absolute oneness, he in turn explained the celebrated Verse of Light, which begins: “God is the light of the heavens and the earth ...” (24:35). For those who understand its true meaning, light is being, just as darkness is nonbeing. The Light that is God is therefore the very being of the heavens and the earth. It alone, and nothing else, truly exists when we speak of the heavens and the earth.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01087

This means that God alone is, together with His Names, His Attributes, and His Acts—that is, His appearances or theophanies. The totality of being is therefore Him, exists through Him, proceeds from Him, and returns to Him. God is not one being alongside or above other beings, even the creatures He has made. He is Being itself, the absolute act of being (wojûd motlaq). Divine oneness is not an arithmetical unity, one unit among, beside, or above other units. For if there were any being other than Him, even created being, God would no longer be the One—the only one who truly is. This in no way abolishes the multiplicity of beings or reduces it to an illusion. The illusion would be to misunderstand how they exist.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01088

What lies outside Being is simply nothingness; the alternative to divine oneness, to God's being alone, is nihilism. To assume the secret of Tawhîd is for a human being to know nothing other than God. This is why theological Tawhîd, if it is not to collapse into its own opposite, must find its fulfillment in the Tawhîd of Being: what our author, following his master Ibn ’Arabî, calls ontological Tawhîd. In doing so, he draws out the teaching of all the mystical theosophers who preceded him in Islam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01089

There is, then, a theological Tawhîd (Tawhîd olâhî). This is outward or exoteric Tawhîd (Tawhîd zâhir), to which the prophets called all humanity: the affirmation of one God who is unconditioned and absolute, free of every limiting determination that would bind Him to particular places or historical circumstances. Its formula is Lâ ilâha illâ’Llâh: there is no god but God. And there is an ontological Tawhîd (Tawhîd wujûdî). This is inward or esoteric Tawhîd (Tawhîd bâtin), to which the initiates—the Friends of God, the Awliyâ—call human beings. They ask us to contemplate Being in its absolute act of being, free from the limitations that appear in the particular forms it brings into existence, for there can be no being other than Being.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01090

To understand the inward meaning of the verse “Everything on earth passes away (fânin); only the Face of your Lord, in glory and majesty, remains” (55:26–27) is to understand that only the One Being is real. The formula here is Laysa fi’l-wojûd siwâ’Llâh: nothing exists but God. We should avoid calling this simply monism, which would invite confusion with modern Western systems that have nothing to do with the matter. Theomonism, or perhaps even theomonadism, would be more accurate.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01091

To illustrate this absolute oneness of Being in its many appearances (mazâhir), Haydar Âmolî uses the example of ink and the letters written with it. Put aside for a moment the particular shapes of the letters, and consider only the ink that gives them their substance. The existence of the letters is then seen to be another way of considering the existence of the ink.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01092

Yet considering them as letters adds no new, independently real existence to that of the ink. In the material reality of their being, the letters are nothing other than ink itself. Writing is ink taking on the form, the particular whatness, of one letter or another. This does not mean denying that there are many different letters; it means understanding how they exist. Conversely, what we directly perceive is never Being in itself, but Being manifested in its forms. We perceive the appearances of Being. In the same way, ink shows itself only in some form (whether in letters, in an inkwell, or even in a blot—the reasoning is unchanged).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01093

The letters would be nothing without the ink, yet the ink does not become a different ink in each of them. In the same way, Being in its appearances does no more than multiply itself by itself (1 × 1). Each time it is the ink itself that exists as this or that letter. Everything is individual, and yet everything is One. This is the transcendent unity of Being (wahdat al-wojûd). Such, for these thinkers, is the relationship between Necessary Being and the forms in which it appears. To lose sight of this is to associate some other being with the One. Then Tawhîd disappears: monotheism turns into idolatry.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01094

The crucial word has just been spoken. The nightmare of the devout Muslim and of the theologian alike is what Arabic calls shirk. It is usually translated as “associating”: associating other gods with God, or associating some other being with Being itself. Perhaps the idea of disintegration better conveys what is involved. The two forms of Tawhîd face a double danger: the disintegration of Being and, as a consequence, the disintegration of the divine. In other words, without the initiates' inward Tawhîd, the outward Tawhîd of naïve monotheism turns into its opposite. Haydar Âmolî distinguishes two kinds of shirk. There is open, manifest shirk (shirk jalî), and hidden, secret shirk (shirk khafî). The first belongs to someone who has never heard the prophets' call and worships this or that particular divinity.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01095

The second is infinitely more subtle. It secretly threatens the literal-minded believer and the scholar of religious Law who rejects the mystics' Tawhîd of Being. Only the person who turns toward Being freed from every limiting determination, and understands that God alone truly is, escapes this hidden, unconscious shirk. Only such a person affirms Unity in its true sense and becomes an ’ârif, a gnostic, one who knows.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01096

But the danger is so subtle, and eats so deeply into the hidden recesses of monotheistic consciousness, that the Prophet declared: “Shirk moves through my community more invisibly than a black ant crossing a black stone on a black night.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01097

No Tawhîd, therefore, is true unless it brings about both the integration of the divine and the integration of Being. Tawhîd in the true sense (haqîqî), rather than in a figurative sense (majâzî), is the theosophical Tawhîd that unites its theological and ontological forms. This is the “Straight Path” (sirât mostaqîm). It is easy to describe, but the difficulty of following it is measured by the difficulty Adam faced in assuming the divine trust. Haydar Âmolî goes so far as to say: “Among a hundred million souls, perhaps only one succeeds, for this Path is more hidden than the mythical Phoenix (the ’Anqâ’ al-maghrib), harder to find than red sulphur or the philosopher's stone.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01098
During the “cycle of prophecy,” from Adam to Mohammad, the “Seal of the prophets,” all the prophets (Nabîs) appeared in order to call (da’wat) creation to theological Tawhîd.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01099

By contrast, during the “cycle of walâyat,” from the Prophet's death until the reappearance of the last Imam, the mission of all the initiates (Awliyâ)—the members of the spiritual hierarchies described earlier, together constituting the Imam's imamate—is to call humanity to ontological Tawhîd. Their task is to deliver people from the hidden, unconscious shirk that is its opposite, however devout the motives behind that error may be.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01100

To understand the position of Twelver Shiite theosophy in relation to religious Law (sharî’at), we must be clear about the following distinction. Theological Tawhîd is what the outward letter of revealed religion teaches, and it applies to this present world because sharî’at itself is limited to the world's present condition. The prophetic mission that brings religious law, and is the source of both sharî’at and theological Tawhîd, has already come to an end in this world. Walâyat, on the other hand—the Imam's power to initiate people into spiritual truth—is eternal. It applies to the present state of the world, to what preceded it, and to what will follow it.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01101

For Shiite theosophers, walâyat precedes prophecy and the prophetic mission, of which it is the origin and source. Just as Manifestation began with walâyat, so its completion must occur in and through walâyat. Or, to put it another way: just as the ordering of being (tartîb wujûdî) began with ontological Tawhîd, so it will end with ontological Tawhîd, because the End is a return to the Beginning. Here we encounter the cyclical pattern of thought shared by all our authors and their rejection of a straight-line conception of evolution. The cycle begins in a reality beyond history and leads back to it. It would therefore be pointless to set a cyclical understanding of history against a “history of salvation.” The doctrine of salvation itself presupposes a cyclical history and a cyclical time.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01102

It is to this integration of Being that the Imam of the Resurrection (Qâ’im) will finally summon humanity. He will not reveal a new sharî’at, but will unveil the hidden meaning of all previous revelations. His reign will be the reign of pure spiritual meaning, of the Eternal Religion (Dîn bâqî, qayyim). Because this religion rests on theosophical Tawhîd, which integrates all being, it will make it possible for humanity to gather again into a single community, as in the beginning of Adam's age. The call to theological Tawhîd, to outward monotheism, ended with the “Seal of the prophets.” Now comes the call to the initiates' inward Tawhîd, to the Eternal Religion whose seal will be the last Imam (Khâtim al-Awliyâ). For Twelver Shiites, that Imam is even now the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01103

There is thus an essential connection between walâyat and inward Tawhîd. Not only do the Friends of God, the Awliyâ, summon humanity to this Tawhîd; the coming of the “Seal” of Muhammadan walâyat must also mark the final establishment of integral Tawhîd, hitherto hidden. It is therefore of the greatest importance not to be mistaken about the identity of the final “Seal” of walâyat. As long as the question is how to explain ontological and inward Tawhîd, Haydar Âmolî remains faithful to Ibn ’Arabî's theosophy, while also using a vocabulary of his own.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01104

But we can understand why he must break with Ibn ’Arabî when he reaches a doctrine on which a Shiite thinker cannot compromise. The coherence—or collapse—of the whole pattern of the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of walâyat depends on it. Our earlier discussion (Book I, Chapter VI) has already shown how deeply this dual pattern is rooted in Shiite consciousness.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01105

We shall return to it (infra, Book VII) in connection with the “Hidden Imam,” whom several Shiite writers identify with the Paraclete promised in the Gospel of John. This identification gives the cycle of walâyat a resonance with the idea of the Paraclete, familiar to so many Western spiritual thinkers since Joachim of Fiore.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01106

To sum up, let us recall that there are two cycles: the cycle of the prophets and their mission of bringing religious laws, and the cycle of the Friends and Beloved of God, the cycle of walâyat as spiritual initiation into the secret of divine friendship. This divine love and favor, this walâyat, is eternal.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01107

As we saw earlier (Book I, Chapter VI, 2), even in the Prophet himself it is the source and foundation of his prophetic mission, whereas that mission, unlike walâyat, is temporary. (The doctrine of the Imams in the reformed Ismailism of Alamût and in Twelver Shiism drew different conclusions from this principle. The former affirmed the Imam's essential precedence; the latter preserved the precedence of the Prophet, but precisely because the walâyat within him is the source of his prophetic state.) Just as prophecy came to an end with the “Seal of the prophets,” who is the Seal of both universal prophecy (motlaqa) and particular prophecy (moqayyada), so walâyat has a double Seal: the Seal of universal walâyat and the Seal of particular, or Muhammadan, walâyat.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01108

It is here that Haydar Âmolî, for all his admiration of Ibn ’Arabî, parts company with him decisively. In this he will be followed by all the Shiite gnostics (’orafâ), however deeply they have themselves absorbed the teachings of the great Andalusian theosopher. Ibn ’Arabî maintains that Jesus (’Isâ ibn Maryam) was the Seal of universal walâyat, while he himself would be the Seal of particular Muhammadan walâyat. On this second point, however, we must express a definite reservation: did Ibn ’Arabî really make that claim? Our own belief is that the dream he had concerned the mystery of his personal destiny, as he himself was to live it, just as every mystic has an individual secret.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01109

To transfer the meaning of this dream to the objective plane of sacred history, as his commentator Dâwûd Qaysarî did, does not seem consistent with Ibn ’Arabî's own understanding. Several contemporary Iranian shaykhs, well acquainted with Ibn ’Arabî's work, share this view. There is also Ibn ’Arabî's own testimony, speaking in veiled terms of his mysterious encounter with the Imam of his time. Clearly, then, he did not identify himself with that Imam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01110

Unfortunately, the first doctrine remains. Ibn ’Arabî clearly states that Jesus is the Seal of universal walâyat, and this is radically incompatible with the understanding of prophecy developed within Islam by Shiism. That understanding requires the Seal of walâyat—the inward reality of the prophetic mission—to be the Imam, and no one else.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01111

Yet Ibn ’Arabî assigns this title to Jesus. He thus makes a prophet, the last great prophet before Mohammad, the Seal of walâyat. This introduces an inconsistency into the fundamental relationship between the prophetic mission and walâyat. It is a confusion that seems to have no purpose other than to make the Shiite doctrine of the Imams disappear, leaving a doctrine of the imamate without an Imam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01112

By contrast, the Shiite theosopher's position is unshakable. The Seal of universal walâyat can only be the First Imam, ’Alî ibn Abî-Tâleb. The Seal of particular Muhammadan walâyat can only be the Twelfth Imam, the awaited Imam, “at present hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his followers”: Mohammad al-Mahdî, son of the Eleventh Imam, Hasan al-’Askarî. For the Muhammadan imamate as a whole, the complete company of the Twelve Imams, is the Seal of walâyat, and the manifestation of integral Tawhîd is bound up with it (see also Book I, note 238).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01113
These indications already suggest the importance of Haydar Âmolî's work in the thought and spirituality of Shiism as a whole.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01114

We shall be better placed to return to the subject when further progress has been made in editing the works of his that we have rediscovered. Understood in its essential ’irfânî character—as Islam's own spiritual knowledge or gnosis—Shiism, whether in Sa’doddîn Hamûyeh or Haydar Âmolî, in Molla Sadrâ or Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î, and whatever their disagreements on other questions, leads us to raise once more, with Haydar Âmolî, the question of Sufism's essential character and meaning. Has non-Shiite Sufism not, in its deepest tendency, aimed at an imamate without an Imam? Has it not transferred everything contained in the doctrine of the Imams to the person of the Prophet, setting aside whatever was incompatible with Sunni religious feeling?
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01115

This question inevitably arises whenever we study the spirituality of Iranian Islam more deeply in the company of those who lived it or who still live it today. Every inquiry into Muhammadan walâyat centers on the idea of the “pole,” the qotb. This mystical pole of the world, which gives a “polar” dimension to every being that enters into relation with it, is the Imam. If the idea of the pole is separated from the Imam and made to stand independently of the doctrine of the Imams, it tends, by that very fact, toward the metaphysical usurpation denounced by Shiite gnostics. For their understanding of the Imams reaches beyond the Imams as historical individuals.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01116

We have already explained that the Twelve Imams—or, more precisely, the Twelve together with the Prophet and Fâtima the Radiant, the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”—constitute the primordial theophany, the first manifestation of the divine. Their spiritual reality as “persons of light” precedes all manifested worlds, and therefore precedes their own earthly appearance, the form in which they become visible in the sensory world. As such, they have a role in bringing the cosmos into being, corresponding to their role in the final return of all things to their origin and of the soul to itself. The Fourteen Immaculate Ones “inhabit” the Shiite spiritual seeker's consciousness. They fill it in waking life and populate the seeker's visions, whether in dreams or in the intermediate state between ordinary waking and dreaming.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01117
We shall see this again (infra, Books V and VI). Haydar Âmolî is himself a particularly representative example of this spiritual type.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
en-book-4-ch-1-s5
5. Visions in the Night Sky over Baghdad and Khorassan
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01118
This spiritual type combines an aptitude for the highest metaphysical speculation with an aptitude for visionary intuition: the perception, through inward sight (basîra), of spiritual forms.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01119

In short, this is everything embraced by the word kashf: discovery, inward unveiling, visionary perception, and knowledge of sacred realities through direct insight. Such experience is a source of theosophical knowledge, which rises above purely philosophical knowledge gained through reasoning (’aql) and the knowledge that formal theology derives from transmitted historical tradition (naql). These last two modes of knowing reach their fulfillment in theosophical knowledge, because the latter can test them against the direct perception of an eyewitness: the shâhid, someone who is “present to” what is known.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01120

Haydar Âmolî places philosophical and theological knowledge in the category of things learned through human teaching and prolonged effort. Theosophical knowledge, by contrast, is above all what a spiritual heir discovers intuitively within himself. It belongs to his own act of being and comes to him as a trust bestowed directly by divine grace. We are dealing, then, with a spiritual type closely related to the ishrâqî tradition exemplified by Sohrawardî and his followers, for whom philosophy has meaning only if it leads toward personal spiritual realization.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01121

In the long introduction to his commentary on Ibn ’Arabî's Fosûs—an introduction which, as we have already said, amounts to a book in its own right—Haydar Âmolî includes a chapter organized according to precisely these stages of knowledge. He follows the same pattern in all his arguments, moving successively through the three stages of naql, ’aql, and kashf: transmitted tradition, reasoning, and direct unveiling. This chapter revisits and expands a corresponding chapter of the Jâmi’ al-asrâr, devoted to the double Seal of walâyat: the Seal of universal walâyat in the person of the First Imam, and the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat in the person of the Twelfth. The arguments accumulate, then finally catch fire as he appeals to direct testimony. They lead to detailed accounts of magnificent visions in which the names of the beings who dominate the visionary philosopher's consciousness are written in blazing letters against the depths of the night sky.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01122

The first arguments, based on theological tradition (naql) and philosophical reasoning (’aql), seek to establish that the Muhammadan imamate is the Seal of walâyat. They recapitulate themes already discussed: the inauguration of the cycle of prophecy with Adam, its completion with the Prophet of Islam as the “Seal of the prophets,” and the way this ending, by that very fact, inaugurates the cycle of pure walâyat. This latter cycle prepares no new sharî’at, no future religious law. It prepares the coming of the one who will unveil the hidden meaning of every prophetic revelation, the “Pole of poles.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01123

The title “Seal of walâyat” can belong only to someone possessing a double inheritance: inheritance by family descent and inheritance in spirit. The earthly bond of kinship is only the visible sign of the union of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones in the eternal fullness of their being. It provides the support and vehicle for the spiritual inheritance bestowed upon the imamate. The Sixth Imam, Ja’far al-Sâdiq, expressly declared that his bond of spiritual closeness (walâyat) to the First Imam took precedence over his bond of descent through the flesh. The eleven Imams are, in turn, the “heirs,” both in eternity and in time.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01124

But the Twelfth, because he completes their sequence, has the privilege of being the heir without qualification—the absolute heir. His brief appearance in this world was followed by the period of his concealment (ghaybat), which will end only with his return, his reappearance.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01125

At this point in the discussion, the Shiite theosopher must face several objections. If the Twelfth Imam is “alive,” why does he not reveal himself? The answer is always the same: the reasons for his concealment lie neither with God nor with the Imam, but with human beings. How many people today would be capable of recognizing him? How many would be ready to sacrifice themselves for his cause? His reappearance cannot occur until consciousness has awakened. And is this awakening of consciousness not itself his reappearance?
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01126

Yet none of this changes what the Imam essentially is. The Imam remains the Imam whether or not people recognize him, for his place and function as the “pole” neither depend nor could depend on their choice or judgment. On the contrary, it is their existence that depends on this pole, even when they do not know it.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01127

But the “Pole” is under no obligation to appear before the appointed Hour of manifestation, when he will take up the cause for which he has been ordained. Through his knowledge, which encompasses all things, the Imam knows the conditions of time and place.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01128

Such, says our Sayyed, is the great certainty binding upon the faith of the pure believers (dîn hanîfî). It rests on a divine necessity, arising from the mission with which God invested His last prophet. From now on there will be no more prophets, but no age can be left “empty,” deprived of the “Pole.” Were the Pole to cease to exist, the whole human world would collapse. Some have said that the awaited Imam will appear one day, but has not yet been born. That evasion is useless. Only people who have understood nothing of the metaphysical necessity for a “pole” of Being in this world could speak in such a way.
